bridge: P04 separated reading data from calculating with it. Start with a function whose expected answers you can work out by hand.
teaching:
### Write the expected answer first

For a total function, choose a tiny input and add it yourself. Then compare the function's returned value with that independent answer. A test that repeats the same faulty calculation as the function may repeat its mistake.

Check a normal case, an empty case, an invalid value and each important boundary. Name the behaviour each test is intended to protect.

### Narrow down a failure

Read the error location and inspect the values reaching it. Reduce a large failing input to a small example that still shows the problem. A debugger can pause execution and show variables; carefully placed temporary output can also help.

Do not solve a failure by deleting the test without understanding the disagreement. The expectation may be wrong, but explain why before changing it.

### Use patterns for the right job

A regular expression describes a text pattern. It can find candidate dates or check a narrowly defined identifier format. It does not automatically understand a full programming language, prove that input is safe or establish that a real date exists.

Some patterns can take excessive time on certain inputs. Keep the accepted format simple and limit input size where appropriate.

### Keep tests repeatable

Use fixed fictional values and mock external services when testing local logic. A mock stands in for a service with a controlled response. Separate those tests from any authorised checks that would contact a real service.

A regex fullmatch requires the whole string to fit the pattern. Search asks whether any matching part occurs inside it. A valid short identifier hidden inside a longer invalid string can therefore pass search but fail fullmatch. Test a newline and overlong input explicitly under the exact pattern.

### Read the pattern and test code

In r"[a-z][a-z0-9]{2,7}", r marks a raw string, useful for patterns containing backslashes. [a-z] matches one lowercase English letter. [a-z0-9] matches one such letter or digit. {2,7} repeats that second part two through seven times. With the first letter, that gives three through eight characters in total. fullmatch returns a match object on success and None on failure; is not None turns that result into True or False.

class IdTests(unittest.TestCase) groups tests using Python’s standard test tools. The test method receives self, the current test object. assertTrue and assertFalse compare a result with the expected truth value; the extra s prints the failing input in the error report. The final if block runs the test tool when you run this file directly. You can reuse this scaffolding while learning classes in P06.

For the port task, first reject text that is not one through five ASCII digits, then convert and check 1 <= value <= 65535. ASCII digits here mean 0 through 9. Python’s and checks the left condition first and skips the right one when the left is False. This avoids converting rejected text with int. The newline escape \n represents a line break, not two ordinary letters.
explanation: The first character must be a lowercase letter. It is followed by two through seven lowercase letters or digits, making total length three through eight. abc! is rejected because fullmatch does not ignore the trailing exclamation mark. A search-based implementation would accept a matching substring and violate the contract.
exercise: Save the example as ids_test.py and run it as a module in IDLE, or with the Python command for your environment. It should report OK. In this disposable copy only, replace fullmatch with search and run again: which expected rejections now pass the validator, and which one does unittest report first? Restore fullmatch. Add "ABC", "a b", "" and "abc\n" to the list that should be rejected; the last contains a newline escape. Predict all four results first. Check that each test’s expected answer comes from the stated identifier rule, not from copying the function’s current result.
solution: With search, both abcdefghi and abc! incorrectly pass: a matching substring is enough. abcdefghi contains the valid-looking prefix abcdefgh, so the eight-character maximum is no longer enforced on the whole input. The rejection loop first passes ab, then fails on abcdefghi; an assertion failure stops that test method, so abc! is not reached. Restoring fullmatch rejects all four added cases: "ABC", "a b", the empty string, and "abc\n" (including its newline). All stated tests then pass. A valid identifier is not by itself proof of authorisation.
challenge: Define valid_port(text) accepting only decimal text whose numeric value is 1 through 65535, with no spaces or sign. Supply tests for "0","1","65535","65536","-1"," 80" and "x".
challenge_solution: Accept "1" and "65535"; reject the others. Validate the text syntax first, then convert and check range. Explain whether non-ASCII decimal characters are allowed by your chosen predicate; an ASCII-only regex [0-9]{1,5} makes the policy explicit. A minimal ASCII policy is: return re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]{1,5}", text) is not None and 1 <= int(text) <= 65535. This accepts leading zeros only within the one-to-five-digit limit: "00080" is accepted, but more than five digits (including zero-padded forms) are rejected before int() runs. Test "0"*5000 and "0"*4300+"1": both return False without raising. An unbounded digit match could let a huge decimal string reach Python’s integer-conversion limit. Add a non-ASCII digit case and a trailing-newline case to distinguish the chosen contract.
example_intro: Save this complete file as ids_test.py using P01’s editor. Run the whole file, rather than only valid_id. A successful run reports one test and OK; it does not print each accepted identifier. The test deliberately checks several inputs inside that one test method.
